passage:
Friday, late

Big fight at dinner. Mama came from the village and within ten minutes we were arguing about the new factory they want to build near his fields. I said it would bring jobs. He said, "You city boys read one article and think you know everything."

I felt my ears burn. I wanted to win. I had numbers ready from my social science project.

Then Siddharth, my cousin, kicked me under the table. And I looked at Mama properly. His hands were shaking a bit around the glass. He wasn't just arguing. He was scared about his land, about the well water.

So I tried asking. "Mama, what are you most worried will happen?" He talked for a long time about the well his father dug. I told him calmly what I'd read about the pollution rules. When he started shouting again, I said, "Mama, I respect you. Let's finish this tomorrow," and went to wash up.

Later he knocked and gave me a laddoo. We didn't agree. But we're fine.

Madhav

qa.q: Where does the family want to build the new factory?
qa.a: They want to build it near Mama's fields.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when Mama called him a city boy?
qa.a: Madhav felt angry and embarrassed, with burning ears, and wanted to win the argument.

qa.q: What did Madhav do when the talk turned heated, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Madhav said he respected Mama and suggested finishing tomorrow, then left the table, which kept the relationship safe instead of trying to win.

qa.q: What is Mama worried about, underneath the argument?
qa.a: Mama is afraid for his land and the well water his father dug, so the argument is about fear, not only politics.

grounding: It shows a teen clashing with his uncle over politics at dinner, listening for the uncle's worry, staying calm and leaving respectfully when it heats up.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 12A, after the mock parliament

Saurabh and Binita have been best friends since Class 6. In the mock parliament this term, they ended up on opposite benches, and it was clear they each genuinely back the real parties those benches stood for. In the first session they argued hard, and at lunch I saw them eat separately for the first time.

On Wednesday they stayed back to finish a project. I heard Binita say, "I don't want to fight about who's right. Can we say why we care instead?" Saurabh said he cares most about jobs for people like his father. Binita said she cares about fair treatment for families like her grandmother's. They were quiet for a while.

Then Saurabh said, "So we're not trying to convert each other?" Binita laughed. "No chance. Deal." They shook hands, very formally.

They were back at the same lunch table on Thursday, still disagreeing, still laughing. I have asked them to co-lead next week's discussion on respectful debate.

qa.q: How long have Saurabh and Binita been best friends?
qa.a: They have been best friends since Class 6.

qa.q: What might Binita have been feeling when she suggested talking about why they care?
qa.a: Binita seemed tired of fighting and worried about losing the friendship, wanting to understand rather than win.

qa.q: What did Saurabh and Binita agree on that protected their friendship?
qa.a: They talked about the values behind their views and agreed not to try to convert each other.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see Binita's reasons after hearing them?
qa.a: Saurabh may see that she cares about fairness for her grandmother's family, just as he cares about his father's work, which makes her view feel less like an attack.

grounding: It shows close friends who back opposite parties, talking about the values behind their views and agreeing not to convert each other so the friendship holds.

passage:
Tuesday night

Elizabeth and I nearly stopped being friends today. Over a city election we can't even vote in.

It started in the bus. She said the new mayor's plan to widen roads was the only way the city would grow. I said it would cut down every tree in the old colony. We got louder and louder. Someone in the back seat started clapping.

At school, I couldn't stop thinking about it. She's been my best friend since Class 4. She taught me to ride a cycle.

At lunch I sat down next to her anyway. I said, "Can we not fight about who's right? Tell me why it matters to you." She said her father loses two hours in traffic every day and misses dinner. I told her about the neem tree outside our window that my Dadi planted.

We didn't change each other's minds. We made a rule: no converting. Just explaining. Then we shared her rajma chawal.

— Irfan

qa.a: She said widening the roads was the only way the city would grow.

Instead she asked Gopika, "Who makes money from me being this angry?" They spent the free period looking up how to check where a video comes from.

Vikas, you forward things fast, I've seen it. Let your Uday Mama tell you about one evening when I was seventeen.

There was a forward on the family chat. A blurry video, men with sticks, and a message: "They are coming to our area tonight. Share with everyone to warn them." Names of a community. My blood boiled. I was sure it was true. I had typed "Share to all" before I even thought.

Your Nani stopped me. She was watching over my shoulder. "Who sent this first?" I didn't know. "Where was it filmed?" I didn't know. "Why does it want you angry?" I didn't have an answer.

We called my maths teacher, who read the local news. He said the video was from years ago, somewhere else entirely. That night, two streets away, a man was beaten because someone believed the same forward.

I never forgot. When something makes you furious that fast, Vikas, it was probably made to. Stop. Check. Then decide.

qa.q: Who stopped young Uday from sharing the forward?
qa.a: Vikas's Nani stopped him; she was watching over his shoulder.

passage:
I'm Jyoti, and in Class 11 I felt like the only person in school who didn't have a team.

Our class group argued about everything: fuel prices, new laws, whose leader was worse. I agreed with one side about some things, like public transport, and with the other side about others, like small businesses. When I said that at lunch, Minakshi rolled her eyes. "You can't have it both ways. Pick one."

I went home confused. Was I just weak? Everyone else seemed so sure.

My Dadu, who reads three newspapers every morning, laughed when I told him. "I'm seventy-two and still learning. Why should you be finished at sixteen?"

So I started reading the editorials from both sides on Sundays, and a book from the library about how policies actually get made. When Minakshi asked again, I said, "I'm still learning. I'll tell you when I know."

She didn't like it. But I felt steadier than I had in months.

qa.a: Jyoti felt confused and pressured, wondering whether not having a team meant being weak.

qa.a: Jyoti started reading editorials from both sides and a library book on how policies are made, because reading widely is stronger than joining a team early.

passage:
Civics teacher's note, Class 10, after the class debate

In the Friday debate, the class split into two loud camps. Yash stayed at his desk. When Ganga, who led one side, called out, "Yash, which side are you? You can't sit on the fence," the whole room turned to him.

He went red. "I agree with some of both," he said. Someone laughed. "Fence-sitter."

After class he stayed back and asked me, "Is it bad that I don't know? Everyone else has a side."

I told him it isn't bad. Knowing you're still learning is honest, and many adults would be wiser if they said it more. I gave him three articles from different viewpoints on the same issue and asked him to tell me next week what each one leaves out.

On Monday he came back with notes in the margins. In the next discussion, when Ganga asked again, he said calmly, "Still learning. But I've read both sides now." Ganga paused, then said, "Okay, tell me what you read."

qa.a: Someone called him "Fence-sitter."

At the school eco-club meeting, Shreya could barely sit still. The lake behind the colony had turned green and smelly, and she'd seen dead fish at the edge that morning. "We should march to the municipal office tomorrow!"

Shreya still wanted to do something bigger. They planned a Sunday clean-up of the lake edge with permission from the residents' association, and a petition with facts and photos.

On Saturday night, Shreya left a note on the fridge for her parents: "Lake clean-up, 7 to 10 a.m., with eco-club and Mrs Rao. Phone on." Then she set her alarm.

Dear Amma and Appa,

I'm writing this so you can read it properly before we talk.

You know about the paper leak in the state board exam. Thousands of us studied for months, and now some people bought the questions. I'm so angry I can't sleep. Imran and some seniors are organising a silent march on Saturday from the school gate to the education office to ask for a fair re-exam.

I want to go. I'll walk with the teachers, keep my phone charged, and send you my location every half hour. If anything feels unsafe, I'll leave and call you.

Can we talk tonight after dinner?

Dolma

Santosh, your friends are asking you to march for something you don't understand? Sit. Your Lakshmi Ammamma has a story from her college days.

It was 1979, I was seventeen, in Madurai. All my friends were joining a rally. Big slogans, big banners. My best friend, Selvi, said, "If you don't come, you're against us." I didn't even know what the rally was about, only that everyone was shouting.

I loved those friends. I wanted to stand with them so much my chest ached. But I didn't understand the demand. So I asked my history lecturer to explain both sides. I read the pamphlets from both groups at the library.

In the end I didn't go. I didn't agree with half of what they were demanding. Selvi didn't talk to me for a week.

Then she came back. She said, "At least you know why you didn't come. Half of us didn't know why we did."

Understanding first, Santosh. Belonging will wait for you.

You want to know why I don't go to rallies without checking who runs them now? I'm Yamini. In Class 11, a college senior, Asif, came to our tuition centre and said they needed "young faces" for a protest about the bus fares. "Bring your school ID, it looks good on camera."

About forty of us went. When we got there, he told the school kids to stand at the very front, right at the police barricade. The college students stayed behind us. There was no water, no first-aid, nobody told us where to go if it got rough.

When the crowd started pushing, my friend got pressed against the barricade and started crying. I felt pure panic. Asif was shouting slogans from the back and didn't even look at us.

I grabbed her hand and we squeezed out through a side lane. I called my father. He came in fifteen minutes.

A real leader puts the youngest at the back and has a plan. And you're always allowed to leave.

"You're not going to the march tomorrow?" Ishita asked, watching her brother Hrithik pace the balcony.

"I want to. The exam fairness thing matters." He rubbed his face. "But what if the police do something? Or the principal suspends everyone? Papa would kill me."

In Class 10, part of our school building had cracks you could put a finger through. The seniors started a petition to the management asking for repairs before the monsoon. I'm Tushar, and I wanted to sign more than anything. But I was terrified.

A boy the year before had been called to the principal's office for "creating trouble." My parents had worked hard to get me into that school. What if I lost my place?

I told Jeevan sir, our class teacher, that I was scared, and that I felt like a coward for it.

He said, "Being scared means you understand there could be a cost. That's honest, not cowardly." Then he showed me the school's own rulebook: students were allowed to submit written petitions to management. Signing was within the rules. Shouting at the gate would be a different matter.

I signed. My hand shook, but I signed. The repairs started in June. Nobody was punished.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 12, Monday

Payal came in upset. There is a large protest in the city this weekend about the tree cutting for the metro extension. Her friend Anand is going. Her parents have said no, firmly. "They treat me like a child," she said.

I asked what exactly her parents had said. After a pause she told me: her mother had been caught in a crowd crush at a rally years ago and was hurt. Payal had heard the story before but never connected it.

We talked about how her parents' "no" came from fear, not from thinking her cause was silly. I asked what else she could do for the trees.

She came back on Thursday with a plan. She wants to write an article for the school magazine and a letter to the city paper, and help Anand's group raise money for saplings through a bake sale. She told her parents all of this, and that she would not go to the protest.

Her mother offered to help with the baking. Payal looked lighter.

qa.q: What is the protest this weekend about?
qa.a: It is about the tree cutting for the metro extension.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she first came in?
qa.a: Payal felt upset and frustrated, feeling that her parents treated her like a child.

qa.q: What safer ways did Payal find to support the cause?
qa.a: Payal planned to write for the school magazine and the city paper, and to help raise money for saplings with a bake sale.

qa.q: Why might Payal's mother be so firm about the protest?
qa.a: Her mother was hurt in a crowd crush at a rally years ago, so her fear for Payal is real and personal.

Wednesday night

Aai and Baba said no to the farmers' support rally in town on Sunday. Straight no. I shouted that they didn't care about anything, and Baba left the room.

Omkar is going. His parents said yes. That made it worse.

Later, Aai came and sat on my bed. She said, "Last year at the market protest, a boy from Omkar's colony got hit by a stone. I lay awake for two nights thinking it could be you." Her voice was small.

I hadn't known she thought about that.

So I told her I understood, and that I still care about the farmers. I said, "What if I don't go, but I organise a food and blanket collection at school for the farmers' families? And I'll write a letter to the local paper." She said she'd help me with the collection box.

Baba came back in and said, "That's more useful than one more body in a crowd anyway." I'm still a bit annoyed. But it's a real plan.

Nitin

passage:
Last year, during the climate campaign, I nearly broke. I'm Shreya. I was running the school's plastic-free drive, making posters till two in the morning, answering messages during class, skipping lunch to count bottles.

If I rested, I felt guilty. Like the planet was burning and I was lying on my bed. When my mother told me to sleep, I snapped at her.

Then I failed a chemistry test. And one afternoon I fell asleep on the bus and missed my stop by six stations.

Vishal, who co-led the drive with me, sat me down at lunch. "You're doing the work of five people. If you burn out, the drive stops. We need you in December, not just now."

That hit me. Causes don't need one person doing everything for a month. They need people who last.

So we split the jobs among eight people. I made a rule: no campaign messages after nine. I started sleeping again. The drive kept going. So did I.

qa.q: How many stations did Shreya miss after falling asleep on the bus?
qa.a: Shreya missed the stop by six stations.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when trying to rest?
qa.a: Shreya felt guilty, as if resting meant ignoring a burning planet.

qa.q: What changes helped Shreya keep going, and why?
qa.a: Splitting jobs among eight people and stopping campaign messages after nine helped, because rest made Shreya able to last.

qa.q: How does Vishal see Shreya's overwork?
qa.a: Vishal is worried that Shreya will burn out and the drive will stop, so he wants Shreya to pace the work.

grounding: It shows a teen pouring everything into a cause and feeling guilty about resting, who learns that rest and studies are part of long-term commitment.

passage:
Class teacher's note, 9B, Thursday

Arnab has been running the animal shelter donation drive almost single-handedly since October. He is at the collection table every break, on the phone with the shelter after school, and I have seen him doing the spreadsheets in maths class. His homework has been missing for two weeks.

Today his friend Tenzin came to me quietly. "Arnab hasn't eaten lunch all week. He says every rupee matters and he can't stop." I asked Arnab to stay back.

He looked exhausted. When I asked about rest, he said, "If I rest, dogs go hungry. I feel guilty even sitting here."

I told him the shelter needs people who will still be helping next year, not someone who collapses in November. We made a rota together: Tenzin and four others each take a break shift. Arnab keeps the spreadsheets, but only on Wednesdays.

He agreed, reluctantly. At lunch I saw him eating, with Tenzin at the table.

qa.q: How long has Arnab's homework been missing?
qa.a: His homework has been missing for two weeks.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when asked about rest?
qa.a: Arnab felt guilty and anxious, as if resting would mean dogs going hungry.

qa.q: How did the class teacher help Arnab keep the cause going without burning out?
qa.a: The teacher made a rota with Tenzin and four others and limited the spreadsheets to Wednesdays, so Arnab could rest and still help.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see what Arnab is doing?
qa.a: Tenzin is worried about Arnab not eating, which is why he quietly told the teacher.

grounding: It shows a teen pouring everything into a cause and feeling guilty about resting, and learning that rest is part of long-term commitment.
